analysis.one_liner: Sunsets the federal income tax code after 2008 unless Congress passes a replacement.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2006 with 7 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shut off every federal tax under the Internal Revenue Code — income taxes, corporate taxes, estate taxes — for years beginning after 2008, keeping only Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes. It creates a commission to recommend a replacement, such as a flat tax or national sales tax, and tells Congress to approve a new tax system by July 4, 2008 or vote to bring the old code back. The bill never says what the new system would be, so taxpayers would not know what would replace the income tax before the old one expired.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the clearest immediate winners would be high earners and corporations, who pay the largest share under the progressive income tax, which the bill ends outright while leaving payroll taxes untouched. Households that pay little or no income tax would gain little unless Congress adopted a replacement that protects them. A commission-dominated process heavy on private-sector members would also give businesses and tax-policy interests large influence over the design of whatever came next [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the Internal Revenue Code for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2008, keeping only self-employment, Social Security (FICA), and Railroad Retirement taxes [S3].

It establishes a 15-member National Commission on Tax Reform and Simplification, required to include at least two small-business owners, to study whether the income tax should be replaced with a flat tax, a national sales tax, or another system, and to report recommendations to Congress within 18 months [S2][S3].

It sets a deadline of July 4, 2008 for Congress to approve a new federal tax system, and if no new system is approved, requires a vote to reauthorize the existing code — a forcing mechanism designed to prevent the tax code from surviving by inertia [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Whoever would bear the burden of the unspecified replacement tax. If Congress adopted a national sales tax or another consumption tax, the burden would fall proportionally harder on lower- and middle-income households, who spend most of what they earn, while the bill eliminates the progressive income tax that falls most heavily on high incomes. In the interim, ending the income tax without an identified replacement would open a hole of roughly a trillion dollars a year in federal revenue, threatening funding for everything funded by income taxes, from defense to retirement programs [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary taxpayers under an unknown replacement

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the entire income tax code without naming any replacement, so the largest change to federal finance in modern history would rest entirely on what Congress might pass later — an enormous gamble with household finances and government funding [S3].

The bill's own provisions conflict: Section 3 unconditionally terminates the income tax after 2008, while Section 5 says Congress must vote to reauthorize the code if no new system is approved by July 4, 2008, leaving unclear whether the tax code could actually be revived [S3].

Replacing the progressive income tax with a consumption tax such as a national sales tax would shift the tax burden toward lower- and middle-income families, who spend a larger share of their income, and toward retirees living off savings — a cost an honest supporter of simplification must acknowledge [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — a simpler tax code that costs less to comply with — is legitimate, and a deadline can break legislative inertia. But this bill buys urgency by blowing up the current system before anyone knows what replaces it. The commission it creates is designed to study the question, yet the termination date is fixed regardless of what the commission finds, and the bill is internally inconsistent about whether the code can even be revived. As drafted, it trades a known, if frustrating, tax system for an undefined one whose burden could easily land on the people least able to pay.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2006 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Johnny Isakson introduced the Tax Code Termination Act on January 20, 2006 [S1][S5].
Seven Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the 109th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers kept the tax system they knew: because the bill never advanced, the progressive income tax stayed in place and no untested replacement was imposed. The existing tax-preparation and compliance industries also kept their market intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo taxpayers and the tax-prep industry

for.name: Sen. Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 20, 2006 and sought to force a deadline for replacing the income tax code.

for.name: 7 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support within the majority party but not enough to move it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never considered it; the record shows no hearings, markups, or committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 7 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so the partisan split rests on sponsorship alone.

industries.note: The bill ends the progressive income tax, which falls most heavily on high earners and corporations, while keeping payroll taxes in place. Any replacement, if enacted, would likely shift more of the burden toward consumption, which weighs on ordinary households.

A wholesale replacement or radical simplification of the tax code would shrink the market for tax preparation, software, and compliance services that exists because the code is complex. The bill's stated purpose is to make that complexity disappear.

If the replacement were a national sales tax, retailers would become collection agents for a federal tax, taking on new compliance costs. The bill leaves the replacement undefined, so the effect is speculative either way.
